extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of journalism history; historians of American Revolutionary-era media
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter describing newspapers' roles, practices, and influence in the American colonies during the Revolutionary period, with examples of publishers, papers, and government interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to publish within the law
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish with the utmost freedom, whatever can be warranted by the laws of your country (John Adams: 'Be not intimidated... publishing with the utmost freedom, whatever can be warranted by the laws of your country').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Adams' exhortation is used as a normative standard: printers should not be intimidated by charges of sedition or politeness and should publish important information for the public interest, exposing avarice and ambition where necessary. The passage frames legal warrant as the boundary of press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power and reach of newspapers (influence on public opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers exerted a powerful influence; 'their appeals reached practically every threshold' and they made 'the sense of national life... intense and vivid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation and penetration into households made papers able to shape national sentiment; the text cites widespread readership and the use of cited authorities (Montesquieu, Locke, Burke) as evidence of intellectual influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and boldness of publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should be 'bold and fearless' — the example of Benjamin Edes and John Gill shows the importance of courage in maintaining principles during crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book praises publishers who risked threats and financial loss to agitate against oppressive measures; bravery is framed as a key quality for effective patriotic journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should avoid falsehoods; Rivington's Gazette was criticized as a 'Lying Gazette' for 'disregard for the truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative warns that false statements damage credibility and provoke organized responses (resolutions, boycotts). Publishers were warned by contemporaries to be more truthful; accuracy is tied to reputation and political legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and credibility of editorial stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency in political alignment and editorial voice matters; Gaine's 'double-dealing' (taking both sides in the same issue) undermined credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching sides or presenting contradictory accounts in the same issue is cited as an 'anti-pattern' that led readers and communities to reject such papers; steadfastness of position (even if partisan) preserved trust among a paper's constituency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic viability: circulation and advertising as sustaining factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial health (circulation numbers, advertising revenue, patronage) determines a paper's survival and capacity to influence (example: Gazette circulation fell from ~2,000 to 400; printers employed many people and required income).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include appeals for subscribers to pay debts, reliance on patronage (royal or political salaries), and the economic incentives for printers to accept government support. Financial pressures could affect editorial choices and longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as an instrument of government propaganda or supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments recognized and sought to use the press as an 'engine' of influence (Serle: government might employ 'able superintendents of the press' and 'allowing salary... would be too trifling to mention').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text documents official attempts to supervise, subsidize, or authorize newspapers to shape public opinion in favor of the government; this constitutes both a production strategy and a normative warning about state influence on journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchdog role: exposing ambition, avarice, malfeasance
rubrics_metrics.description: The press has a duty to publish and point out 'avarice and ambition' when public interest, liberty, and happiness are at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Adams' endorsement of exposing misconduct is presented as a standard for patriotic journalism: newspapers should hold powerful figures to account, even at risk of being called seditious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational resilience: ability to relocate and continue publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers and papers must maintain continuity under threat by moving presses and types (examples: Massachusetts Spy moved to Worcester; Edes moved press to Watertown; New York Packet moved to Fishkill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative treats continuity of publication during military occupation or danger as a positive criterion — the ability to keep issuing papers despite evacuation, suspension, or confiscation signals commitment and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisanship, audience trust, and the role of faction
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers were often Whig or Tory and readership followed factional lines; in 1774, of 31 English papers in the colonies, 21 were Whig. Readers sought and believed newspapers 'with avidity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partisanship shaped both content and uptake: alignment with a political faction determined circulation, local resolutions (boycotts) against opposing papers, and the use of papers to hold or convert public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political oversight, censorship, and employment restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional authorities monitored and disciplined printers (Committee of Safety ordered Loudon to explain a reprint; chairman said they would 'not employ any person who shall do things inimical to the cause of American freedom').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text documents that wartime governments exercised selection and punitive measures affecting who could be official printer or receive patronage — a de facto standard that political loyalty could determine access to official printing roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation management and community sanction (boycotts, resolutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities and committees passed resolutions to drop or boycott papers judged false or harmful (e.g., resolutions against Rivington; committees calling on him to account for false statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective sanctions (boycotts, public denunciations) are depicted as informal regulatory mechanisms by which communities enforced journalistic standards and punished perceived misconduct.
